failure_modes.description: The assumption that intersections can model their 'value' to the network is completely unsubstantiated and ignores the complexity of traffic flow dynamics
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic flow is governed by fluid dynamics principles, not economic valuation. Intersections cannot 'know' their network value without global information, which contradicts the decentralized nature of the proposed system

failure_modes.description: The claim that competitive dynamics lead to global optimization directly contradicts established research in traffic engineering
failure_modes.evidence: Decades of traffic engineering research have shown that competitive signal timing leads to Braess's paradox outcomes where increased capacity actually reduces network performance

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis fails to account for boundary conditions where traffic patterns exceed system capacity
failure_modes.evidence: Market mechanisms fail catastrophically when demand exceeds supply, which is exactly what happens during peak traffic hours in urban networks

failure_modes.description: Numerous existing distributed traffic signal control systems already implement similar competitive resource allocation
failure_modes.evidence: Systems like SCATS and SCOOT have been using distributed optimization with competitive elements for decades, showing that this approach doesn't provide significant improvements over traditional methods

failure_modes.description: The proposed system would create exactly the inefficient allocations described in the falsifier condition
failure_modes.evidence: Market-based systems naturally create winners and losers. High-demand corridors would capture all available green time while side streets would be chronically under-served, precisely the failure condition

failure_modes.description: Traffic flow does not respond to timing changes as if making economic choices
failure_modes.evidence: Driver behavior follows established traffic flow theory (like the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards model), not economic decision-making. Vehicles cannot 'choose' different routes based on signal timing in real-time
